lessons.title: MVC, MVVM, and MV

quickCheck.prompt: In MVVM, what's the main testability advantage of the view model over logic left inside a UIViewController?
quickCheck.explanation: A view model holds no reference to a view or view controller, so it can be constructed and asserted against directly. Logic embedded in a view controller normally requires standing up the full view hierarchy just to exercise it.

options.text: It runs on a background thread automatically
It can be instantiated and tested without any UI, since it holds no reference to a view or view controller
It replaces the need for a model type
It automatically conforms to Codable

lessons.title: Dependency Injection
lessons.body:
Dependency injection is handing a type its collaborators from outside, instead of letting it construct or look them up itself. The seam that creates — a place where a test can substitute something else — is the whole reason DI matters for testability.

### Three ways in

- **Constructor injection** — pass dependencies through `init`; the type can't exist without them, so nothing is optional or forgettable. This is the default: explicit, and enforced by the compiler.
- **Property injection** — set a `var` after construction. Useful when a dependency isn't known at init time, but it leaves a window where the property is `nil` and the type must guard against it.
- **Environment injection** — SwiftUI's `@Environment`, an ambient value resolved by the view tree rather than passed explicitly. Convenient for values many views need, but it hides the dependency from the initializer, so it's easy to forget a view needs a value a preview didn't supply.

### Protocols as seams

Injecting a concrete type only helps if that type is itself replaceable. Injecting behind a protocol is what actually buys the test double:

```swift
protocol ProfileStoring {
    func fetch(id: String) async throws -> Profile
}

final class ProfileViewModel {
    init(store: ProfileStoring) { self.store = store }
    private let store: ProfileStoring
}
```

A test now hands in a stub `ProfileStoring` and never touches the network — the same seam the Testing topic's test doubles rely on.

### Manual DI vs a container

Most apps get by wiring dependencies by hand at one composition root near app launch. A container automates that wiring via registration and resolution, which pays off once the graph is large enough that manual wiring becomes its own burden — and costs a layer of indirection until then.

> KEY: Injection without a protocol boundary still leaves rigid, hard-to-test code — the protocol is the part that actually buys a seam.

quickCheck.prompt: Which form of dependency injection makes a dependency's requirement explicit and enforced by the compiler, rather than something that can be silently missing?
quickCheck.explanation: Constructor injection passes the dependency through init, so the type simply cannot be constructed without it — the compiler rejects a missing argument. Property and environment injection both allow a window where the dependency isn't set yet.

options.text: Constructor injection — the type can't be constructed without it
Property injection
Environment injection
Reaching for a shared singleton instance

lessons.title: Coordinators and Navigation

quickCheck.prompt: Under the coordinator pattern, what does a view do instead of directly navigating to a concrete destination view?
quickCheck.explanation: The view expresses intent — through an event or closure — and lets the coordinator decide where that leads. If the view still built the destination itself, the coordinator would only be watching, not deciding, which defeats the point.

options.text: It expresses intent, e.g. through an event or closure, and lets the coordinator decide where that leads
It still creates the destination view itself, just with a coordinator watching
It stores the destination in UserDefaults
It calls the destination view's initializer directly, same as without a coordinator

lessons.title: Modularization
lessons.body:
A modularized app splits into local Swift Package Manager targets — one per feature or layer — instead of one flat app target holding everything. The payoff isn't philosophical; it shows up as measurable build and test behaviour.

### Boundaries are the actual point

A package only exposes what it marks `public`; everything else is invisible to its consumers by construction, not by convention. That's stronger than a comment saying not to call something from outside — the compiler enforces it. A networking package that only exports a protocol and hides its `URLSession` plumbing can change its internals freely, since nothing outside the package could have depended on them.

### Build-time and testability

Swift Package Manager caches build output per module, so changing one feature's package recompiles that package and whatever depends on it — not the whole app. It also forces the dependency graph to be explicit and acyclic: a package can't secretly reach into another's internals, so the layering that MVVM or DI only describes in theory gets enforced at the build-graph level too.

```
Sources/
  AppCore/        // models, no UI
  Networking/     // depends on AppCore
  ProfileFeature/ // depends on AppCore, Networking
  App/            // depends on all feature packages
```

### The cost of over-modularizing

Every boundary is also a tax: crossing it means something must be `public`, tracked in your head even without formal versioning, and sometimes duplicated where a type is needed on both sides of a boundary that shouldn't have existed. A two-screen app split into six packages spends more effort managing seams than the seams save. Modularize along boundaries already changing independently, not preemptively along every plausible seam.

> KEY: A module boundary earns its cost when it isolates something that changes on its own schedule — otherwise it's just extra ceremony around the same code.

quickCheck.prompt: What does marking a type internal (the default) rather than public inside a Swift Package Manager module actually enforce?
quickCheck.explanation: Access control at a package boundary is compiler-enforced: an internal type simply cannot be referenced outside its module, unlike a comment or naming convention that a caller could ignore.

options.text: That no code outside the module can reference it, checked by the compiler rather than by convention
That the type cannot be used in unit tests
That the type is automatically thread-safe
That the module builds faster

questions.prompt: What is the classic criticism of Apple's MVC pattern in a UIKit app?
questions.explanation: Nothing in MVC limits what a controller may do, so it becomes the default dumping ground for fetch logic, delegate callbacks, and presentation formatting — growing into a massive view controller that's hard to test and hard to change safely.

options.text: The view can directly modify the model
The controller becomes a dumping ground for logic that has nowhere else to go, growing into a massive view controller
MVC does not support more than one view on screen
MVC only works in SwiftUI, not UIKit

questions.prompt: In MVVM, what does the view model hold, and why does that matter for testing?
questions.explanation: A view model holds presentation state and logic with no reference to a view or view controller, so it can be instantiated and asserted against directly, with no UI involved.

options.text: Presentation state and logic with no reference to a view or view controller, so it can be instantiated and tested without any UI
The persisted database schema for the screen
Only formatting helpers, never state
A reference to the concrete view it's bound to, so it can update it directly

questions.prompt: ProfileViewController creates its own APIClient instance directly inside the class. What's the practical problem this causes?
questions.explanation: Because the client is created inline as a concrete type, there is no seam to substitute a test double — testing loadProfile means going through a real network call, since nothing about the design allows swapping in a stub.

options.text: There's no seam to substitute a test double, so testing loadProfile means hitting a real network call
APIClient must be declared as a struct for this to compile
The completion handler will never be invoked
UIViewController subclasses cannot own stored properties

questions.prompt: Which of these is the main reason constructor injection improves testability?
questions.explanation: Routing every dependency through init forces it to be explicit, so a test can supply a stub or fake in its place without touching production wiring or the real implementation.

options.text: It forces every dependency through init, so a test can supply a stub or fake without touching production code
It makes the class run faster at runtime
It removes the need for protocols entirely
It is required by the compiler for every class

questions.prompt: A type depends on a protocol rather than a concrete class for its data source. What does that buy a test?
questions.explanation: Depending on the protocol means the test can hand in any conformer, including a stub or fake with no real implementation involved, instead of being locked to the concrete production type.

options.text: The test can hand in a stub or fake conforming to the same protocol, with no real implementation involved
The protocol makes the type run on a background thread automatically
It guarantees the type is safe to share across threads
It removes the need to write any tests at all

questions.prompt: What's a common pitfall of reaching for a singleton, a globally shared instance, as a dependency?
questions.explanation: A singleton is a hidden global dependency: callers reach it directly by name instead of receiving it, so there's no seam left for a test to substitute something else in its place.

options.text: It hides a global dependency that's hard to substitute in a test, since callers reach it directly instead of receiving it
Singletons cannot be written in Swift
Singletons are always safe to access from any thread by default
Singletons make a type automatically encodable

questions.prompt: What problem does the coordinator pattern solve?
questions.explanation: A coordinator moves navigation decisions out of the view and into a separate object, so a view only has to express that something happened, not what screen comes after it.

options.text: It moves navigation decisions out of the view, so a view doesn't need to know what screen comes after it
It replaces the need for a model layer
It makes SwiftUI views render faster
It is a way to avoid ever using protocols

questions.prompt: PhotoUploader constructs its own APIClient inside the class, so a test can't replace it. Which refactor makes it injectable?
questions.explanation: Defining a protocol for the send call and injecting a conformer through the initializer creates the seam a test needs; the concrete APIClient can then be swapped for a stub or fake in tests while production code still passes the real one.

options.text: Define a protocol covering the send method, inject a conformer through PhotoUploader's initializer, and let a test pass in a stub or fake
Mark APIClient as final so it can't be subclassed
Make upload synchronous instead of async
Add a conditional compilation branch that skips the network call in debug builds

questions.prompt: What is a concrete benefit of splitting an app into local Swift Package Manager modules, versus one flat app target?
questions.explanation: Access control at a package boundary is enforced by the compiler rather than by convention, and Swift Package Manager caches and reuses build output per module, so unrelated changes rebuild less of the app.

options.text: Access control at the package boundary is compiler-enforced, and build output can be cached and reused per module, so unrelated changes rebuild less
It removes the need to write unit tests
It automatically makes every type safe to share across threads
It is required before an app can ship on the App Store

questions.prompt: A SwiftUI screen just displays fields from an observable model with no extra formatting or logic. What does introducing a dedicated view model buy here?
questions.explanation: A view model that only forwards the model's properties one-for-one adds little; the MV approach of binding the view directly to the model fits a screen this thin, and the ceremony only earns its cost once there is real presentation logic to isolate.

options.text: Little — a view model that only forwards the model's properties one-for-one is mostly ceremony for a screen this thin
A guaranteed performance improvement, since observable models always require a view model
It is required, since SwiftUI views cannot read an observable model's properties directly
It removes the need for a model type entirely

questions.prompt: What problem does a repository, or data-source abstraction, solve for a screen that needs data?
questions.explanation: A repository gives the rest of the app one interface for fetching and saving data, hiding whether it actually comes from network, disk, or an in-memory cache behind that single boundary.

options.text: It gives the rest of the app one interface for fetching and saving data, hiding whether it comes from network, disk, or cache behind that boundary
It replaces the need for a model layer
It guarantees the data returned is always fresh
It is a SwiftUI-only concept with no UIKit equivalent

questions.prompt: OrderSummaryViewModel reads UserDefaults.standard directly. What's the smallest change that makes currencyCode() testable without touching the real UserDefaults?
questions.explanation: Introducing a narrow protocol for reading the stored preference and injecting a conformer through the initializer creates a seam; a test can then hand in a stub that returns a fixed value instead of going through the real UserDefaults.

options.text: Introduce a narrow protocol for reading the stored preference, inject a conformer through the initializer, and hand tests a stub that returns a fixed value
Mark currencyCode() as a static method
Rename the UserDefaults call to a computed property with the same body
Wrap the call in a do/catch block

questions.prompt: Compare SwiftUI's environment injection to passing a dependency through a view's initializer, from a testability and clarity standpoint.
questions.explanation: Environment injection is convenient for ambient values many views need, but it hides the requirement from the initializer's signature, so a preview or test can be silently missing a value the view actually needs; initializer injection makes the requirement explicit and checked by the compiler.

options.text: Environment injection hides the dependency from the initializer's signature, risking a silently missing value; initializer injection makes the requirement explicit and compiler-checked
They are functionally identical in every respect
Environment values can never be overridden in tests or previews
Initializer injection only works for value types, not classes

questions.prompt: A coordinator represents navigation as an array of route values bound to a navigation stack's path. Why does this make deep links easier to support?
questions.explanation: Handling a deep link becomes parsing the URL into one or more route values and setting the path to match — reusing the exact mechanism already used for a normal push, rather than needing a separate deep-link-only code path.

options.text: Handling a deep link becomes parsing the URL into route values and setting the path to match, reusing the same mechanism as a normal push
The navigation stack only accepts deep links, never manual navigation
It removes the need to parse the URL at all
Route values must be sent over the network for this to work

questions.prompt: CheckoutViewModel reads PurchaseManager.shared directly inside refreshEntitlement. What does this cost the type in terms of testability?
questions.explanation: Because the shared instance is reached directly rather than injected, there's no seam to substitute a fake subscription state — a test can't set up a premium or non-premium scenario without going through the real shared PurchaseManager.

options.text: There's no seam to substitute a fake subscription state, since the shared instance is reached directly instead of being injected
isPremium can never be read from a SwiftUI view
refreshEntitlement() must be declared async for this code to compile
Reaching the shared instance makes the class unable to be declared final

questions.prompt: What's the benefit of a unidirectional data flow, state down, events up, over letting a child view mutate a parent's state directly?
questions.explanation: With state changing in exactly one place, tracing why a value changed means looking at that one path instead of checking every view that might have mutated it directly.

options.text: There's exactly one place state changes, so tracing why a value changed means looking at one path instead of every view that might have mutated it
It makes the app run correctly without any model layer
It is required for an observable model to compile
It removes the need for any state at all

questions.prompt: Compare sharing behaviour across unrelated types via a protocol extension against sharing it via a common base class.
questions.explanation: A protocol can be adopted by classes, structs, and enums, and a single type can conform to several protocols at once; a base class forces a single-inheritance hierarchy and only works for classes.

options.text: A protocol lets classes, structs, and enums all adopt the behaviour, and a type can conform to several at once; a base class forces single inheritance and only works for classes
Base classes are always faster to call at runtime
Protocol extensions can never provide a default implementation
The two approaches are interchangeable with no real trade-off

questions.prompt: ProfileView only sends events like didTapFollowers; it never appends to path itself. What pattern is AppCoordinator implementing here?
questions.explanation: This is the coordinator pattern: the view expresses intent through events, and a separate object owns the decision of where those events lead, keeping the view itself unaware of the concrete destinations.

options.text: The coordinator pattern, since the view expresses intent through events and a separate object decides where those events lead
The singleton pattern
The repository pattern
Dependency injection specifically, rather than a navigation pattern

questions.prompt: A settings screen has one toggle and no async work. A teammate proposes a full MVVM view model with a protocol-backed store for it. What's the strongest critique?
questions.explanation: The layered abstraction exists to make something replaceable or testable, but a single toggle bound straight to state has nothing worth isolating yet — the cost of the abstraction isn't paying for anything here.

options.text: The added layer buys testability for logic that doesn't exist yet — a single toggle bound straight to state doesn't need a seam
MVVM cannot be used for a settings screen under any circumstances
A view model always requires a persistence framework
Protocols cannot be defined for a type with a single stored value

questions.prompt: Besides the missing seam for APIClient, what's the deeper design problem with FeedViewController as written?
questions.explanation: The view controller owns fetching, caching, cell configuration, and image loading all in one class, with no boundary a test could exercise in isolation — verifying any single responsibility means standing up the whole class and its table view.

options.text: The view controller owns fetching, caching, cell configuration, and image loading all at once, with no boundary a test could exercise in isolation
A cell subclass cannot hold an image view as a property
An image cache cannot be used from inside a view controller
The class needs to be declared final for this code to compile

questions.prompt: An app's object graph has grown to dozens of interdependent services, each wired by hand in one composition-root function. What's the strongest case for introducing a DI container at this point?
questions.explanation: The manual wiring function has become its own maintenance burden, where reordering or adding one dependency risks breaking unrelated wiring; a container's registration and resolution mechanics can express the same graph with less coupling between construction steps.

options.text: The manual wiring function has become a maintenance burden of its own, and a container can express the same graph with less coupling between construction steps
Containers make runtime performance measurably faster
Manual dependency injection stops compiling past a certain number of services
A container removes the need for protocols in the object graph

questions.prompt: A two-screen app is split into six local packages, one per screen and one per shared concern. What's the most likely cost of this, beyond initial setup time?
questions.explanation: A two-screen app has no independently changing parts to isolate, so more effort ends up managing package boundaries and public API surface than the split ever saves, since a typical change still touches most of the packages together.

options.text: More effort goes into managing package boundaries than the split saves, since a two-screen app has no independently changing parts to isolate
The app will fail to compile past four packages
SwiftUI cannot render views defined outside the app target
It guarantees faster incremental builds regardless of how the packages are split

questions.prompt: AppCoordinator's initializer reaches directly for AnalyticsClient.shared instead of accepting it as a parameter. What does this specifically cost a test of start(path:)?
questions.explanation: Because the dependency is fixed inside init rather than passed in, a test constructing AppCoordinator has no way to substitute a fake analytics client — verifying that start(path:) logs an event means going through the real shared client.

options.text: A test constructing AppCoordinator has no way to substitute a fake analytics client, since the dependency is fixed inside init rather than passed in
start(path:) can no longer be called from a test target
Route must be declared as a class rather than an enum for this to compile
Reaching the shared instance makes AppCoordinator a value type

questions.prompt: A deep link should open a specific comment inside a specific post, several navigation levels deep. Where should the logic that decides those intermediate levels live?
questions.explanation: The coordinator, or router, that already owns the path array can express the destination as a sequence of route values, the same mechanism used for a normal multi-step push, rather than teaching the view layer to jump levels on its own.

options.text: In the coordinator that already owns the navigation path, since it can express the destination as a sequence of route values, the same mechanism used for a normal push
In the view that renders the comment, since it's closest to the destination
In the URL-parsing code alone, with no involvement from navigation state
It must be handled entirely outside SwiftUI, since SwiftUI cannot process deep links

questions.prompt: A SwiftUI view's body directly parses a JSON response and computes a discount total inline, before passing values to child views. What does this violate, and what's the fix?
questions.explanation: This puts business logic and parsing inside the view layer, which can't be exercised without rendering the view; moving that logic into a model or view model the view merely reads from restores the separation and makes the logic testable on its own.

options.text: It puts business logic and parsing inside the view layer, untestable without rendering the view; moving that logic into a model or view model the view reads from restores the separation
Nothing — a SwiftUI view is expected to own all computation for the screen it renders
It violates the language's access control rules
It means the screen must be rewritten in UIKit

questions.prompt: CachingProfileRepository wraps another ProfileRepository and adds caching in front of it, both conforming to the same protocol. What pattern is this?
questions.explanation: This combines the repository pattern with decoration: callers depend only on the ProfileRepository abstraction, so a caching implementation can wrap the remote one transparently, with neither side aware of the other's concrete type.

options.text: The repository pattern combined with decoration, since callers depend only on the shared abstraction and a caching layer can wrap the remote implementation transparently
The singleton pattern, since CachingProfileRepository holds a private cache
This shows the absence of constructor injection, since remote is a stored property
An anti-pattern, since a protocol should only ever have one conformer

questions.prompt: You're reviewing a PR that adds a five-layer abstraction, protocol, DI container registration, coordinator, repository, and a use-case object, for a screen that reads one static list from the app bundle and never changes. What's the strongest reviewer feedback?
questions.explanation: Every one of those layers exists to make something replaceable or testable, but a static, unchanging bundled list has nothing to substitute and no behaviour worth isolating, so the abstraction cost isn't paying for anything here.

options.text: Every layer exists to make something replaceable or testable, but a static, unchanging bundled list has nothing worth isolating, so the cost isn't paying for anything here
The PR is correct, since adding more layers always improves testability
Static data must always go through a repository regardless of complexity
A DI container is required for any screen that renders a list
